entity.name: William the Conqueror
entity.description: The illegitimate duke who conquered England in a single afternoon. William was the bastard son of a Norman duke and a tanner's daughter, orphaned at seven, nearly murdered as a child, and grew up to win the most consequential battle in English history. He ordered the Domesday Book and died when his horse stumbled on hot embers.

story.name: William the Conqueror
story.description: Bastard child survives assassination attempts, crushes a Norman rebellion, invades England with a fleet of 700 ships, wins the Battle of Hastings, and commissions the Domesday Book. The conquest that remade a nation.

moments.name: A Duke's Illegitimate Son Is Born at Falaise Castle in Normandy
moments.subtitle: His mother is a tanner's daughter, earning him the nickname William the Bastard
moments.description: In late 1028, William is born at Falaise in the Duchy of Normandy, the only son of Duke Robert I and his mistress Herleva, daughter of Fulbert of Falaise—possibly a tanner or embalmer. Because his parents never marry, William is known as William the Bastard throughout his youth. His illegitimacy will haunt his early reign: when he becomes duke at age seven after his father dies on pilgrimage, Norman nobles fight for control of the child. Multiple guardians are murdered, and young William reportedly hides in peasant houses to survive. The bastard boy of Falaise will grow into the conqueror of England.
moments.address: Château de Falaise, Falaise, Normandy, France

moments.name: William Crushes a Norman Rebellion at the Battle of Val-es-Dunes
moments.subtitle: A nineteen-year-old duke fights alongside the French king to secure his own duchy
moments.description: In early 1047, William—roughly nineteen years old—faces a major rebellion led by Guy of Burgundy, supported by the viscounts of Cotentin and Bessin. After barely escaping an assassination attempt at Valognes by fleeing under cover of darkness, William seeks help from King Henry I of France. The two return to Normandy and defeat the rebels at the Battle of Val-es-Dunes near Caen. Shortly after, William proclaims the Truce of God throughout Normandy, restricting the days on which warfare is permitted. The victory marks the turning point in William's control of his duchy, though continuous warfare will follow for another thirteen years.

moments.name: William Defeats and Kills Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Hastings
moments.subtitle: A single October afternoon decides who will rule England for the next thousand years
moments.description: On October 14, 1066, William leads a Franco-Norman army against the Anglo-Saxon forces of King Harold Godwinson at Senlac Hill near Hastings. Harold had been crowned king in January after Edward the Confessor's death, but William claims Edward had previously promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to support his claim. William builds a fleet of roughly 700 ships, crosses the English Channel in September, and meets Harold's exhausted army—which had just defeated a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge. Harold is killed during the battle. The Norman victory reshapes English language, law, architecture, and aristocracy permanently.

moments.name: William Is Crowned King of England on Christmas Day in London
moments.subtitle: Norman soldiers outside mistake the coronation cheers for a riot and start burning buildings
moments.description: On December 25, 1066, William is crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey in London, roughly ten weeks after his victory at Hastings. The ceremony is conducted by Ealdred, Archbishop of York. According to chroniclers, when the congregation shouts its approval, Norman soldiers stationed outside the abbey mistake the noise for an uprising and begin setting fire to nearby buildings. The panicked crowd flees the abbey, leaving William reportedly trembling at the altar as the ceremony is hastily completed. The chaotic coronation inaugurates Norman rule over England—a dynasty that will transform the island's language, law, and culture.

moments.name: William Orders a Survey of Every Landholding in England—the Domesday Book
moments.subtitle: Medieval England's entire economy catalogued in a single volume that still survives
moments.description: In 1086, William commissions what becomes known as the Domesday Book—a comprehensive survey of virtually all landholdings in England, recording their size, ownership, agricultural capacity, and tax value both before and after the Norman Conquest. The survey is conducted with such thoroughness that the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle notes nothing escapes it, not even a single ox or cow. The name Domesday (Day of Judgment) reflects the finality of its assessments—there is no appeal. The manuscript remains one of the most remarkable administrative achievements of the medieval world and survives today in the National Archives at Kew.

moments.name: William the Conqueror Dies in Rouen After His Horse Stumbles on Burning Embers
moments.subtitle: His body swells so badly it bursts the stone sarcophagus at his funeral
moments.description: On September 9, 1087, William the Conqueror dies in Rouen at roughly age fifty-nine. While leading a campaign to punish the French king for raiding the Norman border town of Mantes, William's horse stumbles on hot embers in the burning town, and the pommel of his saddle ruptures his intestines. He lingers for weeks in agony at the Priory of Saint-Gervais in Rouen before dying. William is buried at the Abbaye-aux-Hommes in Caen, which he had founded. His kingdom splits: Normandy goes to his eldest son Robert Curthose, while England passes to his second surviving son, William Rufus.
